Sydney Carton stopped in the street, uncertain where to go. “Tellson’s bank at nine,” he said thoughtfully. “Would it be wise to let myself be seen before then? I think so. These people ought to know that a man like me is here. It is a sensible precaution, and perhaps a necessary first step. But carefully, carefully! I must think this through.”

He had already begun walking toward a destination, but stopped himself. He paced a little along the darkening street, following his idea through all its possible consequences. This confirmed his first judgment. “It is best,” he said at last, making up his mind, “for these people to know that a man like me is here.” He turned toward Saint Antoine.

Defarge had said that day that he owned a wine shop in the Saint Antoine district. Carton knew the city well and had no difficulty finding the place without asking anyone. Once he had located it, he left the narrow streets again and ate dinner at an eating house. Afterward he fell into a deep sleep. For the first time in many years, he drank no spirits. Since the previous night he had taken only a little weak wine, and that night he had slowly poured his brandy onto Mr. Lorry’s hearth, like a man finished with drinking it.

It was already seven when he woke, refreshed, and returned to the streets. On his way to Saint Antoine he paused at a shop window containing a mirror. He made slight adjustments to his loose, untidy neckcloth, his coat collar, and his wild hair. Then he went straight to Defarge’s shop and entered.

The only customer happened to be Jacques Three, the man with the restless fingers and harsh, croaking voice. Carton had seen him on the jury. He stood drinking at the small counter and talking to Defarge and his wife. The Vengeance joined in as though she belonged to the household.

Carton came in, sat down, and ordered a small measure of wine in very poor French. Madame Defarge glanced casually at him, then looked again more sharply, and then more sharply still. Finally she came over herself and asked what he had ordered.

He repeated his request.

“English?” Madame Defarge asked, lifting her dark eyebrows with curiosity.

He looked at her for a moment, as though even one French word took time to become clear to him. Then he answered in the same heavy foreign accent.

The public always saw those elderly, frail gentlemen bowing. People commonly believed that after bowing one customer out, they kept bowing in the empty office until another customer arrived to be bowed in.

The lawyer was sharp enough to realize that the banker would never have expressed his opinion so firmly without being completely convinced. Though unprepared for this bitter pill, he swallowed it. “And now,” said Mr. Stryver, shaking the forefinger he used in court at the Temple in general, “my way out is to make you all the ones at fault.”

This was a trick from an experienced Old Bailey lawyer, and it gave him considerable comfort. “You won’t make me look foolish, young lady,” Mr. Stryver said. “I’ll do that to you.”

So when Mr. Lorry called that night, as late as ten, Mr. Stryver sat among books and papers deliberately scattered about. He acted as though the morning’s subject was the last thing on his mind. He even appeared surprised to see Mr. Lorry, and remained distracted and absorbed in other matters.

“Well!” said the kindly messenger, after spending a full half-hour trying unsuccessfully to bring him to the point. “I have been to Soho.”

“Soho?” Mr. Stryver repeated coolly. “Oh, of course! Where is my head?”

“And I am quite certain,” Mr. Lorry continued, “that what I said in our conversation was right. My opinion has been confirmed, and I give you the same advice again.”

“I assure you,” replied Mr. Stryver with great friendliness, “I’m sorry for your sake, and for the poor father’s sake. I know this will always be a painful subject for the family. Let’s say no more.”

“I don’t understand,” Mr. Lorry said.

“I expect you don’t,” Stryver replied, nodding soothingly as if the matter were settled. “Never mind, never mind.”

“But I do mind,” Mr. Lorry insisted.

“There’s no need, I promise you. I assumed there was good sense where there was none, and admirable ambition where there was none either. Now I have escaped my mistake, and no damage has been done. Young women have made such foolish choices before, often enough, and regretted them afterward in poverty and obscurity. Thinking of others, I’m sorry the matter has been dropped, because it would have been a poor arrangement for my worldly interests. Thinking of myself, I’m pleased it has been dropped, because it would have been a poor arrangement for my worldly interests. I hardly need to say I could have gained nothing from it.”

“Keeping firmly in mind the points I have emphasized—the peculiar voice, the extraordinary agility, and the astonishing lack of motive for such an exceptionally atrocious murder—let us consider the slaughter itself. A woman has been strangled by hand and forced headfirst up a chimney. Ordinary murderers do not use methods like these, and certainly do not dispose of their victims this way. You must admit that thrusting the body up the chimney was something utterly bizarre, something that cannot be reconciled with our ordinary understanding of human behaviour, even if we imagine the most depraved men committing the crime. Think, too, of the strength needed to force a body upward into such an opening so firmly that several people together could barely pull it down!

“Now consider the other signs of phenomenal strength. Thick locks—extremely thick locks—of grey human hair lay on the hearth, torn out by the roots. You know how much force it takes to tear even twenty or thirty hairs from a person’s head at once. You saw these clumps just as I did. Their roots—what a dreadful sight!—were clogged with pieces of scalp. They provide clear evidence of the tremendous power used to pull out perhaps half a million hairs at a time. The old woman’s throat was not simply cut: her head was completely severed from her body, using nothing more than a razor. I also want you to consider the animal ferocity of these acts. I say nothing here of the bruises on Madame L’Espanaye’s body. Monsieur Dumas and his respected colleague, Monsieur Etienne, declared that these were caused by a blunt object. So far, those gentlemen are entirely correct. That object was obviously the stone paving of the courtyard, onto which the victim fell from the window overlooking the bed. Simple as this explanation may now appear, the police missed it for the same reason they missed the shutters’ width. Their discovery of the nails had completely closed their minds to the possibility that the windows could ever have been opened.

“If, along with all this, you have properly considered the strange disorder of the room, we have now brought together several ideas: astounding agility, superhuman strength, animal ferocity, slaughter without a motive, horror so grotesque that it is utterly foreign to humanity, and a voice whose sound was unfamiliar to listeners from many different nations and contained no clear or intelligible syllables.”
